name: Evisceration threads

lead: An evisceration thread is a post in looksmaxxing forums that dismantles another user's claimed height, face rating or lifestyle by comparing their statements with photos and posting history. Its role in the community is verification: members use it to check whether a self-description is accurate.

It resembles online identity checks more generally, such as catfishing investigations, where mismatched photos, backgrounds and details are used to question whether a profile is genuine. No research has examined the thread format itself.

paras: A poster collects the target's screenshots, earlier posts and images, points out inconsistencies, and shares the findings in a dedicated thread, often with a mocking tone. Others reply with agreement or counter-evidence.

Threads centre on named individuals and may include hostile language, and sharing someone's photos can raise privacy and harassment concerns. Targets sometimes respond by deleting accounts or arguing back in the thread.

angle.text: Participants say evisceration threads keep rating and stats discussion tied to evidence, so users get a more realistic picture of where they stand and which advice sources report their own results truthfully. That framing comes from forum participants; the threads themselves are often adversarial.

lead: An evisceration thread is a format on looksmaxxing forums in which one user takes apart another user's claims about their height, looks, relationships, results or backstory, using the target's own photos and posts as evidence. Within the community it is presented as an audit of self-reported stats: participants say the format exposes claims that do not match the pictures, which keeps rating and stat discussion tied to evidence about what people really look like [1][2].

For someone trying to improve their appearance, accurate numbers matter, because advice about height, face rating or progress depends on whether the person reporting them is describing themselves truthfully. Members who start these threads usually frame them as protecting that shared information, and as warning others away from users who sell guides or services on the strength of claimed results [2].

The format is related to practices elsewhere on the internet in which users probe a profile for inconsistencies. Catfishing, the creation of a fake online identity with false photos and details, has well-known warning signs such as mismatched photo backgrounds and inconsistent details, the same kinds of discrepancy evisceration threads highlight [1]. Researchers who study online shaming and doxing describe both the appeal of crowd exposure and its risks of privacy loss, disproportionate punishment and harassment [3][4]. No published research has studied the evisceration format itself.

paras: The thread is created by one user about another. The author gathers screenshots, earlier photos and posts, and presents inconsistencies such as a photo that appears to belong to someone else or statements that conflict across accounts, then invites the forum to respond. Titles follow a standard pattern, 'Evisceration of' followed by the target's username, often with a descriptive label such as larper or grifter [2].

Replies tend to fall into three groups: agreement with additional evidence, defence of the target, and mockery. Some members then post their own 'proof' of their stats, or the target posts a rebuttal in the thread. In community slang, a LARP is a made-up persona or inflated stats, and a larper is someone accused of using one.

Exposure and callout threads are older than looksmaxxing. Wikipedia describes the practice of identifying and publicly shaming people online across forums and social media, and traces doxing back to Usenet lists and 1990s hacker culture [3][4]. Looksmaxxing communities grew out of incel and rating-forum culture that Wikipedia associates with PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, where users submitted photos for ratings on the PSL scale, so a norm of checking claims against photographs was established early [5].

The term evisceration, meaning a thorough dismantling, appears in thread titles on looksmax.org going back several years and across a wide range of targets, from individual users to public figures and groups. Because many such threads are written as insults rather than as evidence reviews, this article describes the verification-style ones, which cite specific discrepancies.

Authors say they are exposing claims that cannot be verified and that the community needs honest stats. A typical thread lists specific allegations: for instance, one forum thread accused a user of claiming different heights across accounts, of wearing coloured contact lenses while claiming natural eye colour, of using a bot account to show dating-app results, and of reselling free guides in a paid course [2]. Targets and their supporters frequently reply that the evidence is selectively presented or that the thread is personal.
Participants also see the format as a warning to newcomers about sellers of looksmaxxing courses and 'rating' services whose credibility rests on their own claimed appearance.

sections.h: Context: self-reported height and online identity
paras: Height is the most common claim checked. In a study presented at the 2007 CHI conference, Cornell researcher Jeffrey Hancock and colleagues compared the profiles of 80 online dating users with measured height and weight and with licence ages; about 52.6 percent of men and 39 percent of women had profile heights more than half an inch off, and men systematically overstated height [6]. A 2023 Frontiers in Psychology survey of Danish men found average self-reported height of 182.19 cm against a population mean of about 180.4 cm for similar ages, a difference of roughly 1 percent that the authors read as modest exaggeration [7].

Catfishing refers to building a fake online identity using false photos and personal details, and its recognised warning signs include refusing video calls, inconsistent photo backgrounds and mismatched profile details [1]. Evisceration threads apply a similar mismatch-hunting method to forum personas.

No studies have examined evisceration threads. Research on neighbouring practices describes mixed effects. Wikipedia's online shaming article reports critics who see public shaming as disproportionate punishment and 'justice of the mob', defenders who argue it can improve behaviour if redemption is possible, and the point that archived content can remain visible long after an incident [3]. Its doxing article lists harms such as harassment and swatting and notes laws against doxing in several jurisdictions, with debate over where exposure of a pseudonymous account ends and doxing begins [4].

Because threads name individuals and circulate their images, they can involve harassment and exposure of personal photos. They often use hostile language toward the target. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article records that on some incel-linked boards users rated below average may be harassed [5]. Posting someone's photos or identifying details on a forum can raise privacy and legal issues in jurisdictions that regulate doxing [4].
No studies found. Related research on self-reported height is summarised above.
